author: sonnet
reason: A explains up front why the steps run in this order and what the dangerous case is (a payment that succeeds after the hold has lapsed), defines every term an outsider needs (service, coordinator, outbox and relay, hold statuses), adds a legend to its flowchart, and adds tables for failures, stored data and what the customer sees, so I would understand both how the system works and why; B's per-step structure and status tree are cleaner, but B gives less of the reasoning.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer a clearer mental model: it explains why the steps run in this order, names Order as the coordinator, defines basic terms like webhook and at-least-once delivery, and ends with a customer-view table and a short list of safety rules, though A is tighter and more internally consistent.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier for an outsider to follow: it explains the current system and why it fails, defines every outside piece it relies on (MailRelay's idempotency key, the broker's delivery rules, owner and claim), says why the design has this shape, and collects every failure case in one table; B assumes more background and adds a shadow-comparison mechanism early, before the basic flow is clear.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for someone new to the project: it explains today's system, what MailRelay and its idempotency key do, why the design takes this shape, and the rules every step must keep, all before the step-by-step flow. A is just as rigorous but more compressed and assumes the reader already knows that context.

author: sonnet
reason: A gives a newcomer more of the picture up front: why the work is happening (CPU and DB contention, about 30 duplicate emails a week), the three types with their volumes and the 60 s requirement in one table, and a clear status-based ownership model. B never says why the work is happening and only brings up the password_reset latency requirement late, though its fixed-at-insert route is cleaner.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer more to stand on: it opens with why the change is being made (contention with checkout, about 30 duplicate emails a week), adds a table of the three types with their volumes and latency requirements, walks the whole flow end to end, and names its residual risks. A has a cleaner ownership rule but assumes more of the original brief.

author: haiku
reason: Document A explains the terms an outsider needs (advisory lock, __Host- prefix, dummy hash, fail closed), gives the exact SQL and step-by-step flows with reasons, and maps every requirement to where it is met. Document B is tighter and does cover CSRF tokens and static-asset exemptions, but it leaves more for a newcomer to piece together.

author: haiku
reason: For an engineer new to this project, B explains more: it defines every term it uses (advisory lock, fail closed, the __Host- prefix), shows the actual SQL, walks through each flow step by step with the reason for each choice, and maps every requirement to where the design meets it, while A is accurate but compressed and assumes the reader already knows the context.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains itself without outside context: it defines unfamiliar terms (advisory lock, dummy hash, sweep, fail closed), gives the full SQL schema, gives the reason behind each choice and each failure response, and settles edge cases such as static files, logout being exempt from the session check and GET /login, whereas B points to numbered requirements the reader never sees and leaves which routes count as protected unclear.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains the unfamiliar mechanisms (advisory lock, dummy hash, middleware, fail closed), gives the full SQL schema and a reason for each failure behaviour, and covers edge cases that A leaves vague: static files, logout being exempt from the session check, GET /login and Retry-After. A's requirement table points to numbered requirements an outsider never sees.

author: haiku
reason: A defines every term a newcomer would need (pod, ReplicaSet, readiness and liveness, holder, bake period), gives the reason for the ordering, and covers each failure path and rollback limit explicitly, while B is tighter but assumes stack knowledge such as workload identity and IAM simulation and explains less of why the system behaves as it does.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but an outsider would understand the system better from it. It defines the stack terms A takes for granted (pod, image, readiness and liveness, maxUnavailable, ReplicaSet, KMS). It also explains why things work: the image alone decides where a pod reads its keys, old pods keep the keys built into their own image so a rollback stays safe until the old keys are revoked, and the cluster will not halt a rollout when keys load but a provider rejects them.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a five-step summary of the whole flow, a map of how its steps are grouped, and definitions for terms an outsider wouldn't know (readiness probe, maxUnavailable, service identity, APP_ENV), and it explains why each step comes in that order, while B is tighter and adds good catches like the consumer inventory and the canary pause but assumes more prior context.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a start-to-finish flow and a map of the steps, defines the rolling-deploy and readiness mechanics an outsider needs (maxUnavailable: 0, what /healthz does today, the service identity), and explains why key decisions were made (old keys are treated as leaked, immutable images keep the old keys, why readiness waits for the keys), so a newcomer understands the system better than with A's tighter but less explained steps.
